notes.h: Key ideas: nationalism, liberalism and the Risorgimento
notes.b: Italian unity was driven by two ideas and fought over by three programmes. Knowing these terms makes the whole story of 1815-1871 easier to follow.
points: Nationalism is the belief that people who share a language, culture and history should form one state. In Italy it meant expelling Austria and uniting the separate states into one country.

Liberalism means constitutional government, an elected parliament and civil liberties. In Italy it was represented by Piedmont's constitution, the Statuto, and by Cavour, so liberal ideas and nationalist ideas often worked together.
The Risorgimento (Italian for 'resurgence') is the name for the movement for Italian unity and independence, 1815-1870.
Nationalists disagreed about what kind of Italy they wanted. Mazzini wanted a unitary republic, so one state with no kings and the people as sovereign.
The neo-Guelphs wanted a federation of Italian states under the Pope. Their name recalls the medieval Guelphs, the papal party.

The moderates, and later Cavour, wanted a constitutional monarchy led by Piedmont. This is the programme that finally won, which is why the split between these three matters for exam answers on success and failure.
notes.tip: Define nationalism and liberalism in your own words and tie each to an Italian example, such as the Statuto for liberalism. Name the three programmes when you explain why early attempts were divided.

notes.b: Napoleon had redrawn the map of Italy, but the Congress of Vienna (the 1815 peace settlement) restored the old rulers and made Austria the dominant power. Italy was a patchwork of states, most under Austrian influence, with the Pope ruling the centre.
points: Napoleon had created a Kingdom of Italy in the north (1805) with himself as king, and his brother Joseph and then Murat ruled Naples. He brought the Code Napoleon, a single centralised administration and the idea of a united Italy, which restored rulers could not entirely undo.

The Kingdom of Piedmont-Sardinia, ruled by the House of Savoy, was the only major state ruled by a native Italian dynasty. It was enlarged in 1815 by Genoa, the former republic, which made it the largest independent state in the north-west.

Austria directly ruled Lombardy and Venetia in the north. Tuscany and Modena had Habsburg rulers, and Parma went to Marie-Louise, Napoleon's Habsburg widow, until 1847, so family ties tied the duchies to Vienna.

The Papal States covered central Italy from Rome to Bologna. The Pope was an absolute monarch (a ruler with unlimited power) as well as head of the Church, with the clergy running the administration, so Italian unity threatened his state.
The Kingdom of the Two Sicilies, ruled by the Bourbons from Naples, covered the south and Sicily. Its kings were Ferdinand I (to 1825), Ferdinand II (1830-59) and Francis II (1859-61).

Austria also had military means. Its fortresses of the Quadrilateral (Mantua, Peschiera, Verona and Legnago) guarded the north, and Field Marshal Radetzky commanded its army in Italy, which Austria used to put down revolts.

The Austrian Empire was multinational, so Italian nationalism threatened it directly. Metternich, its chief minister, said 'Italy is a geographical expression' (1847), meaning he saw a map region and not a nation.

Italy was also divided in society. The economy was mainly agricultural, communications were poor, people felt loyal to their region and spoke dialects, illiteracy was widespread and the south was poor.
notes.tip: Be exact on who ruled where. Say Tuscany and Modena had Habsburg rulers and Parma went to Marie-Louise, rather than calling them all Habsburg princes.

notes.h: The Carbonari and the early risings
notes.b: Opposition to the restored rulers began in secret societies. Their risings in 1820-21 and 1831 all failed, and the reasons for those failures shaped what came next.
points: The Carbonari were a secret society that spread liberal and nationalist ideas among army officers, students and professional men in the 1820s. Being secret kept them safe from the police but also kept them small.

The Carbonari took part in the rising in Naples (July 1820) and the rising in Piedmont (March 1821). Both were crushed by Austrian troops in 1821, after the Congress of Laibach, and the leaders were imprisoned or exiled.

In February 1831 risings broke out in Modena, Parma and the Papal Legations (the northern provinces of the Papal States). They were crushed with Austrian help, and Ciro Menotti, leader of the Modena rising, was executed in 1831.
Louis-Napoleon, later Napoleon III, took part in the 1831 rising in the Papal States as a young man. This helps explain why he later posed as a friend of Italian nationalism.
The early risings failed for several reasons: they were run by small secret groups, had no mass support, had local rather than national aims, had no foreign help and faced Austrian military power.
The lesson Mazzini drew was that Italy needed a national movement with popular support, and this is why he founded Young Italy.
notes.tip: For why early attempts failed, give the causes (small secret groups, no mass support, local aims, no ally, Austrian army) and date each with 1820-21 or 1831.

notes.b: Mazzini was the most influential theorist and organiser of Italian nationalism before 1848. His ideal of a republican, unified Italy shaped the movement even though his methods failed and he was left disappointed in 1861.
points: Mazzini was born in Genoa on 22 June 1805, took a law degree (1827) and joined the Carbonari in 1827. He was arrested in November 1830, imprisoned at Savona and went into exile early in 1831.
In 1831 he founded Young Italy at Marseille. It was a secret society for young men under 40 who swore an oath to work for an independent, united republic, and it spread through branches across Italy.

His ideas were a unitary republic with the people as sovereign, and the motto 'God and the People' (Dio e Popolo). He wanted unity through education and popular insurrection (rising), not through kings or foreign help.
His book The Duties of Man (published in full 1860) put duty to the nation above individual rights, so citizens were asked to serve Italy before themselves.

His risings all failed for lack of popular support: the Piedmont army plot (1833, about a dozen executed), the invasion of Savoy (February 1834), the Bandiera brothers in Calabria (1844), Milan (February 1853) and Pisacane's expedition at Sapri (1857, Pisacane killed).

He founded Young Europe at Bern (April 1834) to link revolutionary movements. He lived in exile in Switzerland, France and, from January 1837, London, which stayed his main base for the rest of his life, where he ran his network of exiles.

In 1848 he returned to Italy. In 1849 he was one of the three triumvirs (joint rulers) of the Roman Republic, with Garibaldi commanding its defence. After 1849 his reputation suffered as risings failed and moderates turned to Piedmont.
His supporters, among them Francesco Crispi and Rosolino Pilo, helped prepare the Sicilian rising of April 1860 and pressed Garibaldi to lead an expedition.
notes.tip: At Ordinary Level, each correct dated statement earns marks, so learn the sequence: birth, Carbonari, exile, Young Italy and its aims, motto, failed risings, Young Europe, Roman Republic, attitude to 1861, death. Don't say 'arrest and exile in 1830': arrest was 1830, exile 1831.

notes.h: Key personality: Giuseppe Mazzini (how he was seen, and his disappointment)
notes.b: Mazzini's later life shows the gap between the idea he gave Italy and the state that was built. Contemporaries and historians judge him differently from how he judged himself.
points: Mazzini was a participant, not a witness: he planned risings and sent agents into Italy, and his writings inspired followers, including Garibaldi.

Contemporaries were divided. Radicals and republicans admired him, Cavour and the monarchists distrusted him, Austria and the Pope saw a dangerous conspirator, and to many moderates his risings wasted lives.
He rejected the monarchical Italy of 1861 as a betrayal, because he had wanted a republic built by the people.

In August 1870 he was arrested on arrival at Palermo while trying to start a republican rising in Sicily, and was imprisoned at Gaeta. He was released in the amnesty after Rome was taken (October 1870).
He died at Pisa on 10 March 1872.

Historians now see him as the prophet and ideologue (thinker who supplies the ideas) of the Risorgimento, who kept the idea of unity alive and inspired a generation. His methods failed and his republic was not achieved.
notes.tip: For Mazzini's contribution, judge it rather than narrating his life: set his ideas, inspiration and Young Italy against his failed risings, rejection of monarchy and disappointment in 1861, then state a verdict. Say he was arrested on arrival at Palermo and imprisoned at Gaeta, not just 'arrested in Sicily'.

notes.h: Moderate alternatives and the hopes raised by Pius IX
notes.b: Not every nationalist wanted revolution or a republic. In the 1840s two writers offered peaceful alternatives, and a new Pope seemed to prove that reform could work.
points: Vincenzo Gioberti, in On the Moral and Civil Primacy of the Italians (1843), proposed a federation of Italian states under the Pope. His followers were called neo-Guelphs.
Cesare Balbo, in The Hopes of Italy (1844), argued for reform and independence led by Piedmont's monarchy, not revolution. Massimo d'Azeglio, a Piedmontese moderate, was Prime Minister 1849-52.
Pius IX was elected Pope in June 1846. An amnesty for political prisoners (1846), a civic guard and some press freedom raised hopes of a liberal Pope who might lead Italy.
This explains the early 1848 mood: many moderates expected reform from rulers and the Pope. When Pius IX turned against the national cause the neo-Guelph programme collapsed.
notes.tip: If asked about the alternatives to Mazzini, name Gioberti's papal federation and Balbo's Piedmontese leadership with their dates, and say which one eventually won.

notes.b: In 1848 revolution spread across Italy and, for the first time, a state went to war with Austria. Austria won in 1848-49, but the failure showed which road unity would have to take.
points: The causes were economic distress, hopes raised by Pius IX and news of the February revolution in Paris. The first rising was at Palermo on 12 January 1848, and rulers granted constitutions: Naples, Tuscany, Piedmont (the Statuto, 4 March 1848) and the Papal States.
The Five Days of Milan (18-22 March 1848) forced Radetzky to withdraw to the Quadrilateral fortresses. Venice rose under Daniele Manin, who proclaimed the Republic of San Marco on 22 March 1848.

Charles Albert of Piedmont declared war on Austria on 23 March 1848, the First War of Independence, with the slogan 'Italia farà da sé' ('Italy will do it by herself'). He was defeated at Custoza on 24-25 July 1848, and an armistice followed in August.
Pius IX refused war against Catholic Austria in his Allocution of 29 April 1848. After the murder of his minister Pellegrino Rossi (15 November 1848) he fled to Gaeta, in the Kingdom of Naples.
The Roman Republic was proclaimed on 9 February 1849. Mazzini, Aurelio Saffi and Carlo Armellini governed as triumvirs from March, and Garibaldi commanded the defence.

Charles Albert was defeated at Novara on 23 March 1849 and abdicated that night; he died in exile in Portugal in 1849. His son Victor Emmanuel II made peace with Austria (Treaty of Milan, August 1849).

French troops under General Oudinot, sent by Louis-Napoleon, then President of France, took Rome at the start of July 1849 after a siege, restored the Pope and kept a garrison there. Garibaldi retreated with about 4,000 men, and his wife Anita died on the retreat (August 1849).
Venice held out until August 1849 (22-24 August), then surrendered after siege, cholera and bombardment.
notes.tip: Keep the Roman Republic (1849, Mazzini) and the Republic of San Marco (Venice, Manin) apart, and don't mix Custoza of July 1848 with Custoza of 1866. Louis-Napoleon crushed the Roman Republic as President in 1849.

notes.h: Why 1848-49 failed and what it taught
notes.b: The failure of 1848-49 matters because it fixed the lessons that later nationalists acted on. It pushed moderates away from Mazzini's way and towards Piedmont.
points: Austria's army was the main reason for defeat, because Radetzky's forces came back from the Quadrilateral and won at Custoza and Novara.
Nationalists were divided between republicans and monarchists, and between different states, which means there was no single leader or plan.
The Pope's withdrawal from the war (April 1848) broke the neo-Guelph hope because it showed a Pope would not fight Catholic Austria, and no foreign ally helped Italy.
The lesson was that Italy could not do it alone, as Charles Albert had claimed, so foreign help was needed.
Piedmont kept its constitution and its flag after 1849, so it became the hope of moderates and the leader of the national cause.
notes.tip: For 'why did attempts after 1852 succeed when earlier ones failed': contrast 1848-49 (no ally, divisions, no strong state) with the later period.

notes.h: Piedmont under Victor Emmanuel II and Cavour: reform and the Crimean War
notes.b: After 1849 Piedmont was the one Italian state that kept its constitution, and under Cavour it became the most advanced state in Italy. Cavour then used the Crimean War to turn Piedmont into a player in European diplomacy.
points: The Statuto Albertino (1848) was kept after 1849, which is why liberals trusted Piedmont. It gave a king, a nominated senate and an elected chamber with a narrow property franchise, and Piedmont kept the Italian tricolour. It was the only constitutional state in Italy after 1849, a refuge for exiles.
The Siccardi Laws (1850), named after the justice minister Giuseppe Siccardi, abolished separate church courts and the right of asylum in churches. This caused conflict with the Papacy.

Count Camillo Benso di Cavour, born in Turin in 1810, was a landowner and journalist who founded the newspaper Il Risorgimento (1847). He was minister of agriculture and commerce (1850), then of finance (1851), and admired Britain's economy and parliament.
He became Prime Minister on 4 November 1852 through the connubio ('marriage'), an alliance with Urbano Rattazzi's centre-left.

He modernised Piedmont with free trade treaties with Britain, France and other states, railway building, banking and credit, agricultural improvement and a reformed army. Its railway network became the largest of any Italian state by 1859, making Piedmont the most advanced Italian state.

Piedmont joined the Crimean War (Britain and France against Russia, 1853-56) in January 1855. About 15,000 troops under Alfonso La Marmora fought at the Chernaya (August 1855), which won Piedmont a seat at the Congress of Paris (February-April 1856).

At Paris Cavour raised the Italian question and the problem of Austria's presence in Italy before the Great Powers. Austria's unfriendly neutrality in the war had cost it Russia's friendship, so Austria was more isolated.
notes.tip: For Cavour at Ordinary Level, learn: Prime Minister 1852, economic reform, Crimean War and Paris, Plombieres, 1859, central Italy, Nice and Savoy, attitude to Garibaldi. Each dated statement earns marks.

notes.b: Cavour knew Piedmont could not beat Austria alone, as 1848-49 had shown. He turned to Napoleon III, who wanted to undo the 1815 settlement.
points: The Italian National Society (1857) was founded by Daniele Manin, Giorgio Pallavicino and Giuseppe La Farina. Garibaldi joined as vice-president. It backed unity under Victor Emmanuel and Piedmont instead of Mazzini's republic, and former republicans such as Manin and Garibaldi supported it.
Napoleon III, Emperor of the French from 1852, wanted to undo the 1815 settlement and posed as a friend of nationalities. He also needed Catholic support at home, so he protected the Pope.
Felice Orsini's bombs in Paris (14 January 1858) aimed at Napoleon III. Orsini was executed after writing to the Emperor urging him to free Italy, which pushed Napoleon III towards action.

At Plombieres (20-21 July 1858) Cavour and Napoleon III secretly agreed that France would fight Austria if Austria appeared the aggressor. Piedmont would get a kingdom of Upper Italy, and France would get Savoy and, less firmly, Nice.

Princess Clotilde, Victor Emmanuel's daughter, was to marry Prince Napoleon (Jerome), Napoleon III's cousin. The marriage, which sealed the alliance, took place in January 1859, and a formal Franco-Piedmontese treaty that month included Savoy and Nice.
The price was the cession of Nice and Savoy to France, which angered nationalists, above all Garibaldi, because he was born in Nice.
notes.tip: Don't write that Plombieres simply gave France 'Nice and Savoy': Savoy was agreed and Nice was left less firmly settled, though both were in the January 1859 treaty. Don't say the National Society was founded by Garibaldi.

notes.h: The war of 1859 and the annexation of central Italy
notes.b: Cavour's plan worked at first: France fought beside Piedmont and Austria lost Lombardy. Napoleon III then stopped the war short of the goal, and central Italy took matters into its own hands.
points: Piedmont mobilised, and Austria issued an ultimatum on 23 April 1859 and began war on 29 April, so Austria appeared the aggressor as the Plombieres deal required. France joined Piedmont, and Garibaldi led volunteers called the Cacciatori delle Alpi ('Alpine Hunters').
The allies won at Magenta (4 June 1859) and at Solferino (with San Martino, 24 June 1859). Napoleon III and Victor Emmanuel II entered Milan after Magenta.
Napoleon III stopped the war because of heavy losses, Prussian mobilisation on the Rhine, Catholic anger in France and fear of a too-strong Piedmont.
He agreed the Villafranca armistice with Franz Joseph on 11 July 1859 without Cavour, who resigned. Lombardy went to Piedmont but Venetia stayed Austrian.
The Treaty of Zurich (10 November 1859) confirmed this: Lombardy was ceded through France to Piedmont.

In central Italy the rulers of Tuscany, Modena and Parma fled and the Romagna rose against the Pope. Cavour returned as Prime Minister in January 1860, and plebiscites on 11-12 March 1860 in Tuscany and Emilia (Modena, Parma, the Romagna) voted to join Piedmont.
The Treaty of Turin (24 March 1860) ceded Nice and Savoy to France in return for Napoleon III's acceptance, and plebiscites in Nice and Savoy followed in April 1860.
notes.tip: Keep these apart: Villafranca (armistice, July 1859), Zurich (November 1859), Turin (March 1860, Nice and Savoy). The Treaty of Vienna of 1866 is a different treaty from the 1815 Congress of Vienna.

notes.h: Garibaldi, the Thousand and the Kingdom of Italy
notes.b: In 1860 an adventure that Cavour neither stopped nor openly backed turned the unification of the north into the unification of most of Italy. Garibaldi supplied the military daring that diplomacy could not.
points: Garibaldi was born in Nice on 4 July 1807 and was a Mazzinian, condemned to death in his absence after the 1834 plot. He spent about 1836-48 in South America, in Brazil and Uruguay, where his Italian Legion wore red shirts, and he defended the Roman Republic in 1849.
After a rising in Sicily the Thousand (about 1,000 men) sailed from Quarto near Genoa on the night of 5-6 May 1860. Cavour neither stopped them nor openly backed them.

They landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860. Garibaldi proclaimed himself dictator in Victor Emmanuel's name at Salemi, won at Calatafimi (15 May) and took Palermo at the end of May, with fighting from 27 May. He then won at Milazzo in July.
Garibaldi crossed to Calabria in August, and entered Naples on 7 September 1860 as Francis II withdrew to Gaeta. The battle of the Volturno followed on 1-2 October 1860.

Cavour feared a march on Rome and French or Austrian intervention, so he sent the Piedmontese army through the Papal Marches and Umbria, avoiding Rome itself, and it defeated the papal army at Castelfidardo (18 September 1860).

At Teano (26 October 1860) Garibaldi handed his conquests to Victor Emmanuel II and went to his island home of Caprera. Plebiscites approved annexation in Naples and Sicily (21 October) and the Marches and Umbria (November).

The first Italian parliament in Turin proclaimed the Kingdom of Italy on 17 March 1861, with Victor Emmanuel II as king (to 1878) and Turin as capital. Cavour died on 6 June 1861, aged 50, and his successors struggled to resolve the southern question.

Garibaldi's slogan was 'Rome or death' (Roma o morte). Italian troops stopped him at Aspromonte on 29 August 1862, where he was wounded. French and papal troops defeated him at Mentana on 3 November 1867.
notes.tip: Calatafimi (Sicily, May 1860), Castelfidardo (Piedmontese army, September 1860) and the Volturno (Garibaldi, October 1860) are easy to confuse. Say the Thousand left on the night of 5-6 May, and that Mentana was French and papal troops, not French alone.

notes.b: Two areas remained outside the new kingdom: Venetia under Austria and Rome under the Pope. Venetia came in 1866 because Prussia defeated Austria, and Rome in 1870 after the French garrison left and Italian troops entered the city.
points: The September Convention (15 September 1864) had France promise to withdraw from Rome, and Italy moved its capital to Florence in 1865.

Italy allied with Prussia on 8 April 1866. Italy lost on land at Custoza (24 June 1866) and at sea at Lissa (20 July 1866), but Prussia beat Austria at Koniggratz (Sadowa) on 3 July 1866 and this forced Austria to give up Venetia.
Venetia was handed through Napoleon III to Italy by the Treaty of Vienna (3 October 1866), and a plebiscite in October 1866 approved it.
French troops left Rome in August 1870 on the outbreak of the Franco-Prussian War, so the Pope lost his protector.
After Sedan (1-2 September 1870), the capture of Rome followed: Italian troops entered through a breach at the Porta Pia on 20 September 1870, and a plebiscite on 2 October 1870 approved annexation.

Rome became the capital in 1871 (July), the third capital after Turin and then Florence. The Law of Guarantees (13 May 1871) offered the Pope privileges, but Pius IX rejected it and called himself a prisoner of the Vatican.
Pius IX had declared papal infallibility at the Vatican Council in July 1870, so his hostility to the new state was strong, and this kept many Catholics apart from it.
notes.tip: Put the capitals in order, Turin (1861), Florence (1865), Rome (1871), and give the cause of each gain: Prussia's victory for Venetia and the Franco-Prussian War for Rome.

notes.h: Obstacles to unity and why attempts after 1852 succeeded
notes.b: A good answer pairs each obstacle with the way it was removed. Early attempts met all the obstacles with none of the answers, while after 1852 the answers arrived together.
points: Obstacle: Austria's military power and its hold on Lombardy-Venetia and the Quadrilateral until 1866. The war of 1859 with France removed Austria from Lombardy only, and the Prussian victory in 1866 that gave Italy Venetia ended the obstacle.
Obstacle: the Papacy and its French protectors until 1870. It was overcome when the French garrison left Rome in August 1870 because of the Franco-Prussian War.

Obstacle: regionalism, local loyalties, no common spoken language, illiteracy and peasant indifference. It was overcome in part by plebiscites and by the enthusiasm of 1860, though the problem remained after 1861.

Obstacle: divisions among nationalists (republicans against monarchists, unitary against federal) and reliance on small conspiracies. It was overcome when the National Society brought many former republicans behind Piedmont, ending the 1848 divisions.
Success factor: Piedmont was a strong leading state, constitutional, modernised and with a regular army, so there was now a real centre for the movement.

Success factor: Cavour's diplomacy (the Crimean War, Paris 1856, Plombieres) isolated Austria and won French help. Foreign help also came from France in 1859, Prussia in 1866 and 1870, Britain's goodwill and Austria's isolation after the Crimean War.
Success factor: Garibaldi's volunteers and popular enthusiasm in 1860 moved faster than a regular army could, for example through Sicily and Naples in a few months.

The roles compared: Mazzini gave the idea and inspiration, Cavour the diplomacy and the Piedmontese state, Garibaldi the military daring and Victor Emmanuel II the monarchy all could accept. A textbook summary of this is the soul, the brain and the sword.
notes.tip: For why attempts after 1852 succeeded, contrast 1820-49 (conspiracies, no strong state, no ally, divisions) with after 1852 and give a concrete example and date for each factor. For the 100-mark essay, structure by stages and judge which factors mattered most.

notes.b: The Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed in 1861, but it started with serious weaknesses. Ordinary Level questions often ask about these problems and not only about how unification happened.
points: The franchise was narrow: only about 2 per cent of the population could vote in 1861, so the state rested on a tiny political class.
'Piedmontisation' meant that Piedmont's constitution, laws, officials and taxes were extended to the whole kingdom. It was a centralised state, not a federation.

The south gained little for peasants. The army fought brigandage in the south for several years after 1861 (roughly 1861-65), and the Pica Law (1863) allowed military courts. This is the southern question.
About three-quarters of Italians were illiterate at the 1861 census. Estimates of how many spoke standard Italian range from about 2.5 to about 10 per cent.
The Pope's hostility kept many Catholics apart from the new state, as Pius IX rejected the Law of Guarantees.
notes.tip: Document questions on the new Kingdom ask who ruled it, what its economy rested on, literacy, the war on brigandage and why Pius IX opposed unity, so learn each fact above with its figure.

notes.h: Assessment: achievements and limits of unification
notes.b: Examiners reward paired judgements: what was achieved against what was left unfinished, and how far each leader's vision won. Name a historian to add weight.
points: Achievement: by 1871 the peninsula was united under one constitutional monarchy with Rome as its capital, and Austria had been expelled.
Limit: unity came largely through French and Prussian victories and Piedmontese expansion, not a popular national rising, and the state was narrow, centralised and poorly integrated.
Achievement for Mazzini: the idea of a united Italy, which he had kept alive, won. Limit: his republican, popular Italy did not, and he was left disappointed.
Limit: the new kingdom stayed mostly agricultural and the south poor. What was extended was Piedmont's constitution, laws and administration, not a modern economy.
Denis Mack Smith (Cavour and Garibaldi 1860, 1954) saw Cavour and Garibaldi as rivals as well as partners, and thought Cavour's aims in 1860 were limited.
Antonio Gramsci (Prison Notebooks, written 1929-35) called the Risorgimento a 'passive revolution' led by moderates that left the peasants out.

Lucy Riall (Garibaldi: Invention of a Hero, 2007) argued that the Garibaldi legend was deliberately created through print and images. Older nationalist and liberal histories saw a heroic, almost inevitable rise of the nation.

Compared with Germany, Italy was also led by one strong kingdom using war and diplomacy, but it relied more on foreign help, ended weaker and less united, and was a constitutional monarchy rather than a Prussian-dominated empire.
notes.tip: Pair every achievement with a limit and end with a verdict. In comparison essays state clearly that Italy relied on foreign help, and name Mack Smith or Gramsci for a historian's view.

keyTerms.definition: The movement for Italian national unification and independence from the 1815 settlement until the capture of Rome in 1870.
A secret society of liberal and nationalist conspirators in Italy in the 1820s, whose risings of 1820–21 and 1831 were defeated.
The secret society founded by Mazzini at Marseille in 1831, which aimed at a unified Italian republic.
The constitution granted by Charles Albert of Piedmont in 1848, which Piedmont kept after the other Italian states had abandoned their constitutions.
The July 1858 secret meeting between Cavour and Napoleon III at which France agreed to support Piedmont against Austria in return for Nice and Savoy.
The armistice agreed between Napoleon III and Austria on 11 July 1859, which gave Lombardy to Piedmont and left Venetia under Austria.
The volunteers who sailed with Garibaldi from Quarto in May 1860 and conquered Sicily and then Naples for Victor Emmanuel II.
The state proclaimed on 17 March 1861 under Victor Emmanuel II, which was extended to Venetia in 1866 and Rome in 1870.
The republic proclaimed in Rome in February 1849, governed by Mazzini and others and defended by Garibaldi until the French captured the city.
The belief that people sharing a language, culture and history should form a single state, which drove the Italian movement for unity.
The doctrine favouring constitutional government and civil liberties, which Cavour and Piedmont's constitutional monarchy represented.

factCards.definition: Mazzini's motto was God and the People, reflecting his belief in a republic built on popular sovereignty.
Mazzini founded Young Italy at Marseille in 1831, a society dedicated to a unified republican Italy.
The Milanese rising from 18 to 22 March 1848 drove the Austrian garrison out of the city.
Piedmont's army was defeated by the Austrians at Custoza in July 1848.
Charles Albert's army was defeated at Novara in March 1849, and he abdicated in favour of his son Victor Emmanuel II.
Piedmont's laws of 1850 removed the separate church courts and some clerical privileges, provoking conflict with the Papacy.
Cavour became Prime Minister of Piedmont in November 1852 and led the national movement until his death in 1861.
The French and Piedmontese victories at Magenta on 4 June and at Solferino on 24 June 1859 led to the armistice that gave Lombardy to Piedmont.
The treaty ceded Nice and Savoy to France, after Napoleon III accepted the annexation of central Italy by Piedmont.
Garibaldi and his Thousand landed at Marsala in Sicily on 11 May 1860 and went on to take Palermo.
Garibaldi entered Naples on 7 September 1860 after the Bourbon king Francis II had withdrawn.

factCards.term: Proclamation of the Kingdom of Italy, March 1861
factCards.definition: Victor Emmanuel II was proclaimed king of Italy on 17 March 1861.
Italian troops entered Rome on 20 September 1870 after the French garrison had been withdrawn, completing the unification of the peninsula.
